General Au-Catalyzed Benzannulation Towards Naturally Occurring
Carbazole Alkaloids from ACHTUNGTRENNUNGMethoxypropadiene
Wangqing Kong, Chunling Fu, and Shengming Ma* [a]
A variety of structurally diverse carbazole alkaloids have
been isolated from different natural sources over the past
years.
[1] The genus Murraya, trees growing in southern Asia,
represents the richest source of carbazole alkaloids from ter-
restrial plants, particularly for 2-oxygenated tricyclic carba-
zole alkaloids (Scheme 1). Some of these compounds show
useful biological activities. For example, in 2000, Boyd
et al.
[2] developed a bioassay-guided fractionation of the ex-
tract leading to the isolation of a new carbazole alkaloid,
siamenol, which shows interesting anti-HIV activity (EC 50 =
2.6 mgm L/C01), reaching 50–60 % maximum protection in the
2,3-bis-(2-methoxy-4-nitro-5-sulfophenyl)-2H-tetrazolium-5-
carboxanilide (XTT) assay from Murraya siamensis collect-
ed in Thailand. 3-Formyl-7-hydroxycarbazole was isolated
from the root bark of Murraya euchrestifolia (Scheme 1).
Extracts of the leaves and bark of Murraya have been used
as a folk medicine for analgesia as well as local anesthesia,
for treatment of eczema, rheumatism, dropsy, abdominal
pain, stomach-ache, toothache, diarrhoea, oedema, thrombo-
sis and stasis of blood, and as an expectorant, anti-convul-
sant, anodyne, and detoxification agent.
[3] Clauszoline-K,
clauszoline-L, clausine-M and clausine-N were isolated from
the stem bark of the Chinese medicinal plant. Clausena ex-
cavata is a wild plant that has been claimed to be useful in
folk medicine as a detoxification agent and for the treat-
ment of snake bites.
[4]
In 2002, Witulski et al. [5] reported a creative approach em-
ploying a rhodium-catalyzed [2 +2+2] cyclotrimerization of
a diyne and an alkyne as the key step to clausine-C starting
from 2-iodo-5-methoxyaniline. However, the regioselectivity
of this step is rather poor (the ratio of isomers is 3.8:1;
step 1 in Scheme 2). In 2006, Knçlker et al.
[6] reported a re-
markable approach for the general synthesis of clauszoline-
K, 3-formyl-7-hydroxycarbazole, clausine-M, clausine-N,
clausine-C, and siamenol by utilization of the palladium-cat-
alyzed intermolecular C /C0N bond formation between 3-me-
thoxyaniline and 1-bromo-4-methylbenzene, followed by in-
tramolecular C /C0C bond formation of the coupling product,
3-methoxy-N-p-tolylaniline, as the key step (step 2 in
Scheme 2). However, there should be a serious issue of se-
lectivity for this type of cyclization of unsymmetric 3-me-
thoxy-N-p-tolylaniline according to the related previous re-
ports,
[7] although it was not discussed in this report. [6] In ad-
dition, large amounts of oxidants, such as Cu ACHTUNGTRENNUNG(OAc)2
(2.5 equiv), DDQ (4.2 equiv), and MnO 2 (26 equiv), are re-
quired to complete the synthesis.
Furthermore, in the first total synthesis of siamenol, [6] the
coupling of 3-bromo-6-methyl-9 H-carbazol-2-ol required
9.5 equiv of prenyl bromide and 12 equiv of Ni ACHTUNGTRENNUNG(cod)2 (cod =
1,5-cyclooctadiene) for six days to yield siamenol in 47 %
yield with a low purity. Thus, the pure siamenol had to be
prepared by preparative HPLC, which makes this method
much less attractive. In 2008, Kuethe et al.
[8] reported a
route employing Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling of a 2-ni-
trobenzenediazonium salt with 2-(methoxycarbonyl)phenyl-
boronic acid to give methyl 3-(2-nitro-3-methoxyphenyl)-
benzoate, which was followed by reductive cyclization to
afford clausine-C and clausine-N. However, it is obvious
that the atom economy is very low and these required re-
agents are not readily available. In addition, the selectivity
is also very low in the step of reductive cyclic amination
(the ratio of isomers is 1.4:1; step 3 in Scheme 2). The regio-
selectivity issue is obviously deterring scientists from easily
obtaining the pure compounds. Thus, for the purpose of sys-
tematic biological screening to discover lead compounds,
highly selective and diverse routes with atom economy to
these naturally occurring carbazoles from readily available
starting materials are highly desirable.
In 2009, we developed a PtCl
2-catalyzed synthesis of car-
bazoles from 1-indoyl-2,3-allenols (Scheme 3). [9] However, it
is difficult to introduce functionalities to the skeleton by
using alkyl-substituted allenols. We envisioned that using

readily available methoxypropadiene as the starting point
would solve this problem by incorporating the methoxy
group in the to-be-formed benzene ring for further manipu-
lation to prepare these 2-functionalized naturally occurring
carbazoles (Scheme 3). The challenges here will be the effi-
cient route to the required allenols and the influence of the
methoxy group on the reactivity caused by the selectivity of
the coordination of the two C =C bonds with the metal. In
this paper, we wish to present such a general strategy to
these naturally occurring carbazoles under Au catalysis.
It is noted that in all the carbazoles prepared in this labo-
ratory, there is no N-substituent. Thus, we must identify a
protecting group for the N /C0H functionality that could be re-
moved after the formation of the carbazole. This task was
not trivial, since most of the classical protecting groups, such
as N-Tosyl and N-Boc, failed to produce the carbazoles due
to the fact that the electron-withdrawing groups on the ni-
trogen atom make the indole electron-deficient, and there-
fore nonreactive towards the current cyclization. Finally we
observed that the benzyl group could be introduced into car-
bazole 2a to afford the N-unprotected carbazole 3a in 53 %
yield with MeLi.
[10] By using potassium tert-butoxide/DMSO
and O 2,[11]the yield for the deprotection is much higher
(87 %), which was applied in further study (Scheme 4).
Interestingly, we synthesized 2,3-allenol 1b conveniently
from the readily available 1-methoxypropa-1,2-diene: the re-
action of 1-benzyl-5-methyl-indole-2-carbaldehyde 4b with
1-methoxypropa-1,2-dienyl lithium, in situ generated from
the treatment of methoxypropa-
diene
[12] and nBuLi, afforded
the required methoxy-substitut-
ed allenol 1b in 70 % yield. [13]
Gladly, the PtCl 2-catalyzed cyc-
lization of 1b under the stan-
dard reaction conditions did
afford carbzaole 2b,
[9] albeit in
a low yield (61 %) probably due
to the presence of methoxy
group. Interestingly, further
screening led to the observation
that 2b was formed exclusively
in a much higher yield (81 %)
with AuCl as the catalyst. Elec-
trophilic bromination of carba-
zole 2b afforded 3-bromocarbazole 5b in 88 % yield as the
only product. Deprotection of the N-benzyl group using po-
tassium tert-butoxide/DMSO and O
2 afforded 6b in 80 %
yield (Scheme 5). Next, we started to establish an effective
coupling protocol: Suzuki cross-coupling reaction of 5b with
pinacol prenylboronate [14] afforded 7b in 72 % yield. How-
ever, in survey of many demethylation conditions, acidic
conditions utilizing Lewis acids, such as BBr
3, afforded a
complicated mixture of several products, probably due to
the intrinsic problem of oxygen anion attack at the allylic
double bond. Many reported protocols were tried for this
purpose: lithium chloride in refluxing DMF ,
[15] sodium ethyl
mercaptide in refluxing DMF , [16] and PhSH in the presence
of a catalytic amount of K 2CO3 in refluxing N-methyl-2-pyr-
rolidone (NMP), [17] but all led to decomposition of com-
pound 7b (path A, Scheme 5). On the other hand, Suzuki
cross-coupling reaction of 5b with pinacol prenylboronate
and demethylation with sodium ethyl mercaptide in reflux-
ing DMF afforded 8b in 60 % yield in two steps. Disappoint-
ingly, deprotection of the N-benzyl group of 8b with potassi-
um-tert-butoxide ( tBuOK) in DMSO under O 2, 2,3-dichloro-
5,6-dicyano-1,4-benzoquinone (DDQ) in CH 2Cl2
[18] or MeLi
in THF [19] all failed to generate siamenol (path B,
Scheme 5). Finally, demethylation of 6b with BBr 3 in
CH2Cl2 afforded 9b in 88 % yield. Initially, we tried the
direct Pd 0-catalyzed Suzuki cross-coupling reaction of 9b
with pinacol prenylboronate but this failed, probably due to
the effect of the free ortho-hydroxyl group. When tert-butyl-
dimethylsilyl (TBS) ether was used for the protection of the
free hydroxyl group, the Suzuki coupling reaction did not
occur. Eventually, we were pleased to note that the protec-

tion of the OH group as acetate, followed by coupling and
instant deprotection in a one-pot reaction afforded siamenol
in 66 % yield (path C, Scheme 5).
Luckily, a similar approach may also be used for the syn-
thesis of allenol 1c . The AuCl-catalyzed cyclization of 1c is
also very smooth under the standard reaction conditions to
afford exclusively carbazole 2c in 83 % yield. The deprotec-
tion of the N-benzyl group with potassium tert-butoxide in
DMSO under O
2 (Scheme 4) afforded 6-bromo-2-methoxy-
9H-carbazole 3c in 72 % yield. Starting from 3c , clauszo-
line-K was synthesized in 54 % yield by the subsequent
treatment with potassium hydride, tBuLi, and DMF to in-
stall the aldehyde functionality;
[20] clausine-N was synthe-
sized in 84 % yield by using the Li–Br exchange reaction
with tBuLi and the subsequent carboxylation with CO 2 ;
methylation of this carboxylic acid functionality in clausine-
N with MeI gave clauszoline-L in 95 % yield with NaHCO
3
as the base. Removal of the methyl group in clauszoline-K
and clauszoline-L by treatment with BBr
3 in CH 2Cl2 with a
modified procedure led to 3-formyl-7-hydroxycarbazole and
clausine-M, respectively (Scheme 6).
[6, 21]
The spectroscopic data of our synthetic compounds, that
is, siamenol (7 steps with 21 % overall yield), clauszoline-K
(4 steps with 22 % overall yield), clauszoline-L (5 steps with
32 % overall yield), 3-formyl-7-hydroxycarbazole (5 steps
with 11 % overall yield), clausine-M (6 steps with 19 % over-
all yield), and clausine-N (4 steps with 34 % overall yield),
from the readily available methoxypropadiene are in full
agreement with those reported for the corresponding natu-
ral products (for detailed information, see the Supporting
Information).
In summary, the approach reported herein has solved the
issue of regioselectivity in all the previous reports.
[5, 6, 8] It is
obvious that these routes may be easily used for large scale
syntheses of these naturally occurring carbazole alkaloids or
diversified highly selective synthesis of their derivatives due
to the substituent-loading capability of both the indole
moiety and allenol functionality for further biological
screening. In addition, this strategy should be general to the
synthesis of other naturally occurring compounds shown in
Scheme 7, based on 2b -o r 5b -type products.
[22] This chemis-
try will be of high interest for organic chemists and medici-

Experimental Section
Typical procedure for the preparation of 9-benzyl-6-methyl-2-methoxy-
9H-carbazole (2 b) : PtCl 2 (2.8 mg, 0.01 mmol), 1b (64.0 mg, 0.20 mmol),
and toluene (2 mL) were added sequentially to a dry Schlenk tube under
a nitrogen atmosphere. After continuous stirring for 24 h at room tem-
perature, the reaction was complete, as monitored by TLC. Evaporation
and column chromatography on silica gel (petroleum ether/ethyl ace-
tate = 20 L) afforded 2b as a solid (36.7 mg, 61 %). M.p. 129–130
8C( n-
hexane/ethyl acetate) ; 1H NMR (300 MHz, CDCl 3): d = 7.94 (d, J =
8.4 Hz, 1 H, ArH), 7.82 (s, 1 H, ArH), 7.30–7.07 (m, 7 H, ArH), 6.86–6.75
(m, 2 H, ArH), 5.41 (s, 2 H, ArCH
2), 3.84 (s, 3 H, ArOCH 3), 2.51 ppm (s,
3 H, ArCH 3); 13C NMR (75 MHz, CDCl 3): d = 159.0, 142.2, 139.0, 137.2,
128.7, 128.6, 127.3, 126.3, 125.7, 123.3, 121.0, 119.6, 116.7, 108.3, 107.2,
93.2, 55.6, 46.5, 21.4 ppm; IR (KBr): n˜ = 2994, 2869, 1635, 1610, 1498,
1492, 1452, 1342, 1296, 1260, 1196, 1168, 1142, 1058 cm /C01; MS (EI)
(70 eV): m/z (%): 302 [ M + 1]+ (23.12), 301 [ M]+ (100); elemental analy-
sis calcd (%) for C 21H19NO: C, 83.69; H, 6.35; N, 4.65; found: C, 83.57,
H, 6.50; N, 4.61.
The reaction of AuCl (21.4 mg, 0.092 mmol) and 1b (604.5 mg, 2.0 mmol)
in toluene (10 mL) at room temperature for 8 h afforded 2b (481.6 mg,
81 %; petroleum ether/ethyl acetate = 40 L).
